title: Rendering pipeline & jank diagnosis
scopeHtml: Scope: how a frame travels from Choreographer to the display, how to read jank evidence (gfxinfo, FrameMetrics, JankStats, Perfetto), and the GPU/bitmap/shader/layer causes behind it. Compose-phase and RecyclerView internals live in other chunks.

questions.promptHtml: What is the frame budget at 60, 90 and 120 Hz, and what actually happens when you miss it by 1 ms?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you understand jank as a deadline miss against a fixed VSYNC grid, not as "the app is slow".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The budget is 1000 ms divided by the refresh rate: about 16.6 ms at 60 Hz, 11.1 ms at 90 Hz, 8.3 ms at 120 Hz. And that budget covers the whole pipeline, not just my code. If I miss by 1 ms, the frame is not shown 1 ms late. It misses that VSYNC, so the previous frame stays on screen for another full period, and the user sees a hitch of 16.6 ms or more.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The display scans out on a fixed clock. A finished frame can only be swapped in at a VSYNC boundary. So presentation time is quantized.

60 Hz grid:  |---16.6---|---16.6---|---16.6---|
frame A:     [work 14ms]            -> shown at next VSYNC  (OK)
frame B:     [work 17.6ms ......]   -> misses it, shown one VSYNC later
user sees:   A A B(late) -> one repeated frame = 16.6 ms of extra stall

The doc-stated numbers are roughly 16 ms / 11 ms / 8 ms at 60/90/120 fps. Show the math: 1000/60 = 16.67, 1000/90 = 11.11, 1000/120 = 8.33. The budget is shared: UI thread work (input, animation, measure/layout, record draw), then RenderThread (sync, issue GPU commands), then GPU, then SurfaceFlinger composition. Apps are scheduled ahead of the target present time, so the "app deadline" is earlier than the VSYNC in which the frame appears. Android vitals calls frames over 16 ms "slow" (roughly) and over 700 ms "frozen"; ANR is 5 s.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "16 ms per frame" as a universal; on 120 Hz devices the same code that was fine can now jank.
  • Forgetting RenderThread/GPU/SurfaceFlinger share the budget.
  • Thinking a 17 ms frame is "1 ms late".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does 90 Hz hurt more than the 5 ms difference suggests? → Every phase gets 33% less time, and low-end SoCs often have no headroom to start with.
  2. What is a frozen frame? → A frame over 700 ms (Android vitals); typical at startup or screen transitions.
  3. Can an app run at a lower rate on purpose? → Yes, the system may pick the rate (VRR/adaptive); the app can hint with Surface.setFrameRate (API 30+). Budgets then change per screen.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "16 ms, don't block main". Senior: states the quantization, the shared pipeline budget, per-refresh-rate budgets, and that it is the p95/p99 tail of frame time that users feel.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed that was "smooth" on 60 Hz test phones janked in the field once 120 Hz flagships became 30% of DAU; the fix was budgeting for 8.3 ms on bind and draw, not only 16.6.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through what the UI thread does versus the RenderThread for one frame in a hardware-accelerated app.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who know "main thread" from people who can say which thread a symptom lives on.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The UI thread runs input, animations, measure/layout, and then records draw commands into display lists. It hands those to the RenderThread, which syncs state, replays the display lists as GPU commands, and swaps the buffer. So a clean main thread does not guarantee a smooth frame: the RenderThread can be the one missing the deadline.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
UI thread:        input -> animation -> measure/layout -> Record View#draw
                                                              |  syncFrameState (UI blocked briefly)
RenderThread:                                    DrawFrame: upload textures, issue GPU cmds, swap buffers
GPU:                                                               execute -> fence
SurfaceFlinger:                                                                    compose -> HWC -> display

A display list is a recorded sequence of draw ops (drawRect, drawBitmap...) rather than pixels. Since API 21 (Lollipop) the RenderThread exists so animations such as ripples and some property animators can continue even while the UI thread is busy. During syncFrameState the UI thread is blocked so the RenderThread can safely copy state; a bitmap upload can also occur around then. The RenderThread can block on IPC to acquire a buffer, or on eglSwapBuffers when the GPU queue is full.

In Perfetto you look for Choreographer#doFrame on the main thread and DrawFrame on RenderThread. Long Record View#draw points at custom draw code or CPU bitmap painting; long DrawFrame points at texture upload, large paths, clipPath, saveLayer, shaders or GPU saturation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Profiling only method traces on main thread and missing RenderThread cost.
  • Assuming Compose changes this: Compose still ends in the same UI-thread-records, RenderThread-replays model.
  • Believing GPU work is on the UI thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the UI thread blocked during sync? → So the RenderThread copies display lists/properties consistently.
  2. What can run without the UI thread? → RenderNode property animations (e.g. view alpha/translation via RenderNode, ripple) can be driven by RenderThread.
  3. How do you see RenderThread stalls? → Perfetto DrawFrame, Texture upload, eglSwapBuffers/dequeueBuffer slices, and GPU frame durations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "UI thread draws, RenderThread uses GPU". Senior: names the sync point, display lists, and the specific RenderThread-only costs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team spent a week optimizing main-thread binds; the real stall was 12 ms texture uploads of 4000x3000 hero images on RenderThread.

questions.promptHtml: How do VSYNC and Choreographer drive a frame, and in what order do Choreographer callbacks run?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mental model needed to read doFrame slices and to reason about when work should be scheduled.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SurfaceFlinger/DisplayEventReceiver delivers a VSYNC signal to the app only when the app has asked for a frame (scheduleVsync). Choreographer then runs doFrame on the main looper and executes callback queues in a fixed order: input, animation, (insets animation), traversal (measure/layout/draw), commit. Nothing happens if nobody invalidates, which is why idle apps do zero frames.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
View.invalidate() / requestLayout() -> ViewRootImpl.scheduleTraversals() posts a sync barrier and a CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL on Choreographer -> Choreographer requests the next VSYNC -> on VSYNC, doFrame(frameTimeNanos) runs. Order of callback types: CALLBACK_INPUT, CALLBACK_ANIMATION, CALLBACK_INSETS_ANIMATION (API 30+), CALLBACK_TRAVERSAL, CALLBACK_COMMIT. The sync barrier means ordinary main-looper messages wait until the traversal runs, so a long doFrame also delays all your Handler.post work.

Choreographer logs "Skipped N frames! The application may be doing too much work on its main thread" when doFrame starts late by 30+ frames (threshold in AOSP: SKIPPED_FRAME_WARNING_LIMIT = 30; verify for your target API). Compose hooks in via withFrameNanos/MonotonicFrameClock, which is itself a Choreographer frame callback.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Choreographer.getInstance().postFrameCallback { frameTimeNanos ->
    // runs in CALLBACK_ANIMATION phase of the next frame
    // keep it tiny; it is on the critical path
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing heavy work in postFrameCallback.
  • Thinking Choreographer ticks continuously at 60 Hz regardless of invalidation.
  • Mixing the app's frameTimeNanos with wall-clock time.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the main looper seem frozen during long traversals? → Sync barrier blocks non-async messages until the traversal.
  2. What are app vs SurfaceFlinger VSYNC offsets? → Both are phase-shifted from hardware VSYNC so app, then SF, then display pipeline overlap (the Android Developers blog describes different wakeup offsets).
  3. What is frameTimeNanos in the callback? → The intended VSYNC timestamp, not the time you actually started; the delta is your "late start".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "Choreographer syncs to VSYNC". Senior: invalidate to scheduleTraversals to barrier to doFrame, callback order, and the late-start delta.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A custom view posting Handler.post per scroll event starved behind sync barriers; moving to postFrameCallback coalesced work into one per frame.

questions.promptHtml: Explain buffer queues, triple buffering, SurfaceFlinger composition and HWC. Where can jank appear after my app finishes drawing?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Reveals if you know that "my frame is done" is not "frame is on screen".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each window has a BufferQueue: the app dequeues a buffer, renders into it, queues it with a GPU fence. SurfaceFlinger latches the newest ready buffer each VSYNC and composes layers, preferably with the Hardware Composer (HWC) overlays and otherwise with GPU. Extra buffers (triple buffering) let the app keep working while one is on screen and one is being composed, at the price of latency. After my app is done jank can still come from GPU not finished, SurfaceFlinger missing its own deadline, or the HAL presenting late.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App (producer)   dequeue -> render -> queue(fence) ---+
                                                       v
BufferQueue     [ buf A ][ buf B ][ buf C ]   (3 = triple buffered)
                                                       v
SurfaceFlinger  latch at VSYNC -> compose (HWC overlay or GPU/client comp) -> present

With only two buffers, if the app misses once, the pipeline stalls and the next frame also slips (a cascade). A third buffer absorbs one miss but adds a frame of input latency. On Android 12+ apps send buffers to SF via BLAST transactions. HWC composition is cheap in power; falling back to GPU ("client") composition for many layers, blurs, rounded corners on certain panels or protected content costs GPU time and appears as SurfaceFlinger deadline misses.

Perfetto FrameTimeline classifies this: SurfaceFlingerCpuDeadlineMissed, SurfaceFlingerGpuDeadlineMissed, DisplayHAL, PredictionError, plus app-side AppDeadlineMissed and BufferStuffing.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Blaming app code for SurfaceFlinger-side misses (other apps/layers like PiP or blur contribute).
  • Thinking more buffers is free.
  • Ignoring that SurfaceView/TextureView bypass part of the normal path.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can GPU composition jank while my app is fast? → SF CPU+GPU composition time exceeded its deadline.
  2. What do fences do? → Let the producer/consumer know when the GPU has finished with a buffer without blocking CPU.
  3. How do you find SF-side jank? → Perfetto FrameTimeline jank type and SurfaceFlinger tracks on the Actual timeline.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "SurfaceFlinger composes layers". Senior: BufferQueue, fences, HWC vs client composition, latency vs stall trade-off, and who owns each miss.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A video-call app with three overlapping translucent layers pushed an older device into GPU composition; jank vanished only after removing a full-screen translucent scrim.

questions.promptHtml: What categories of jank does Android distinguish (missed deadline, buffer stuffing, GPU...), and how does each change what you do next?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you triage by evidence rather than "optimize everything".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On Android 12+ FrameTimeline labels each janky frame: App Deadline Missed, Buffer Stuffing, SurfaceFlinger CPU deadline missed, SurfaceFlinger GPU deadline missed, Display HAL, Prediction Error, and a rare Unknown. App Deadline Missed is mine to fix on UI thread or RenderThread. Buffer stuffing is queueing frames faster than they are shown, so latency, not necessarily visible stutter. The SF and HAL types are mostly system or device issues, though my layer count or GPU load can trigger them.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Type Meaning (per Perfetto docs) First action
AppDeadlineMissed App took longer than budget from Choreographer wakeup to later of GPU completion or post Trace UI thread and RenderThread slices
BufferStuffing App queues new frames before earlier ones presented; latency, may still meet deadline Check for producer running ahead; reduce queued work, check frame pacing
SurfaceFlingerCpuDeadlineMissed SF main thread ran long Check other layers/processes, composition strategy
SurfaceFlingerGpuDeadlineMissed CPU+GPU composition too long; GPU work late Reduce GPU load: overdraw, blur, layers
DisplayHAL SF sent on time, HAL presented a vsync late Mostly device/vendor
PredictionError Scheduler prediction drifted from hardware vsync Mostly platform

There is no separate "GPU jank" type; GPU shows up through AppDeadlineMissed (RenderThread waiting on swap) or the SF GPU type. FrameTimeline needs Android 12 (S) or higher. Older devices: infer from dumpsys gfxinfo and slice durations.

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating every jank type as app bug.
  • Counting buffer stuffing as dropped frames.
  • Using it on Android 11 and lower where the data doesn't exist.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you query it? → Perfetto SQL on actual_frame_timeline_slice with jank_type.
  2. Why might SF-side jank be your problem? → Your layer count/blur/translucency forces expensive composition.
  3. How do you separate your jank from system noise at scale? → Segment by device/OS and app-attributable type; JankStats gives app-side only.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "dropped frames". Senior: triages by FrameTimeline type before touching code.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard showed 4% janky frames; 60% were DisplayHAL on a single OEM and not actionable, redirecting the effort to the 1.5% genuine AppDeadlineMissed.

questions.subtopic: dumpsys gfxinfo and Profile GPU Rendering
questions.promptHtml: How do you use dumpsys gfxinfo and Profile GPU Rendering to get a first read on jank?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Practical first-5-minutes tooling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <package> prints totals: rendered frames, janky frames and percent, percentile frame times, and counts like missed vsync and slow UI thread. Add reset before the run so I get only my scenario, and framestats for per-frame timestamps. Profile GPU Rendering (on screen as bars) shows per-frame stage bars against the 16.67 ms line. Both are cheap triage; I follow with Perfetto for the cause.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Workflow: adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <pkg> reset, perform the exact gesture, adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo <pkg>. Output includes "Janky frames: N (x%)", 50th/90th/95th/99th percentile frame times, and reason counters such as "Number Missed Vsync", "Number High input latency", "Number Slow UI thread", "Number Slow bitmap uploads", "Number Slow issue draw commands" (names per recent releases; verify on your device). The bar colors (Android 6+ per docs): Swap Buffers (CPU waiting on GPU), Command Issue, Sync & Upload, Draw, Measure/Layout, Input Handling & Animation, Misc/VSync Delay. Tall Input & Animation in a LazyColumn often means per-item state mapping during scroll. Always on a release-like build; debuggable builds disable ART optimizations.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo com.example.app reset
# scroll the feed for 10 seconds
adb shell dumpsys gfxinfo com.example.app

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not resetting, so startup frames pollute the numbers.
  • Measuring a debug build.
  • Using it on an emulator with software GL.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does Swap Buffers high mean? → CPU waiting on GPU: too much GPU work.
  2. gfxinfo says 3% janky; is that fine? → Depends on the gesture and percentiles; compare with a baseline per device.
  3. How do you automate? → Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric instead of scraping text.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: turns on the bars. Senior: resets, scopes the gesture, reads percentiles and reason counters, then escalates to Perfetto.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Before/after numbers from gfxinfo on a fixed scroll script ended an "it feels faster" argument in code review.

questions.promptHtml: FrameMetrics vs JankStats: what does each give you, and how would you use them in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Production observability of jank, not just local profiling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: FrameMetrics (API 24+) is the platform callback with per-frame timings: input, animation, layout/measure, draw, sync, command issue, swap, total. It gives raw durations but no verdict. JankStats (androidx.metrics:metrics-performance) is built on it, adds a jank heuristic (default: a frame longer than 2x the current refresh interval, tunable with jankHeuristicMultiplier) and UI state tagging, so I can say "jank happened while LazyList was Scrolling on screen X".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• JankStats uses FrameMetrics on API 24+ and an OnPreDrawListener fallback below. One instance per Window; createAndTrack(window, listener); disable tracking in onPause.
  • OnFrameListener runs on the FrameMetrics thread (API 24+), not main. Return fast. The FrameData object is reused, so copy fields you need.
  • On API 31+ FrameDataApi31.frameOverrunNanos shows time past the deadline; FrameDataApi24.frameDurationCpuNanos shows non-GPU time.
  • State: PerformanceMetricsState.getHolderForHierarchy(view).state?.putState(key, value); use unique keys per list; use putSingleFrameState for one-shot events. In Compose update state from a LaunchedEffect + snapshotFlow, not during composition.
  • Aggregate on device (counts, percentiles per state), upload periodically. Do not log every frame.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val jankStats = JankStats.createAndTrack(window) { frame ->
    if (frame.isJank) {
        // copy needed values; FrameData is reused
        bucket.add(frame.frameDurationUiNanos, frame.states.joinToString { "${it.key}=${it.value}" })
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing I/O or allocations in the listener.
  • Keeping a reference to FrameData.
  • Leaving tracking enabled in background.
  • Stale state: forgetting removeState.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why 2x refresh as default? → Rendering time is not fully precise, so a buffer avoids noise; adjust for tests.
  2. Does JankStats tell you why? → No, only where/when; you need Perfetto to find why.
  3. How to make dashboards trustworthy? → Segment by device tier, refresh rate, OS; track jank frames per scroll-second, not raw counts.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "it reports jank". Senior: threading, reuse, state tagging, aggregation, and pairing field data with a lab repro.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: State tags revealed jank concentrated in "Checkout/PromoCarousel=Scrolling" rather than the whole app, shrinking the investigation to one screen.

questions.contextHtml: A shopping app (2.5M DAU, 40% on 3 GB RAM mid-range phones, 60 Hz) gets complaints: "first scroll through the home feed stutters, then it's smooth". Vitals shows slow frames 9% on that screen versus 2% elsewhere. The feed is a RecyclerView of cards with a 1080x1080 product image each. Server recently switched image responses from 600 px to original-size JPEGs (about 2000x2000). Perfetto on a Redmi-class device shows most janky frames have Texture upload(id) 2048x2048 slices of 6-11 ms in DrawFrame, while main-thread doFrame is 5 ms. Memory profiler also shows allocation spikes.
questions.promptHtml: What is going on and how do you fix it without a server rollback?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Optimize onBindViewHolder and move image loading to a background thread." The decode is already background; the stall is on the RenderThread upload, so this fix targets the wrong thread.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Did slow frames start with the server change (timing correlates)? Which loader and does it request target size? Are bitmaps HARDWARE config? Does second scroll stay smooth (cache hit means upload already paid)? Which devices?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ask server/CDN to serve a width-parameterized rendition (or add w= param) as hot fix; or cap decoded size client-side.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) oversize bitmaps cause large texture uploads on first display; (b) decode on main thread (ruled out by trace); (c) GC pressure from large allocs; (d) overdraw (red herring, flat trace shows GPU fine).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto: Texture upload(id) WxH slice sizes vs image view size 360x360 px; dumpsys gfxinfo "Slow bitmap uploads" counter; Memory profiler allocations; Layout Inspector for view size.
  5. Root cause: Each new bitmap is uploaded to the GPU as a texture the first time it draws. A 2048x2048 ARGB_8888 is 204820484 = 16.8 MB; uploading it takes several ms and blocks the RenderThread (and briefly the UI thread at sync). Three new cards per scroll step means 3 uploads in a frame, exceeding 16.6 ms. Second scroll is smooth because textures are cached.
  6. Fix: Short term: request size(width, height) matching the view; downsample on decode. Long term: Coil/Glide with target sizing and Bitmap.prepareToDraw() after decode (API 24+) so upload happens early on idle RenderThread; prefer hardware bitmaps (API 26+) which decode directly to GPU memory; prefetch next page images. Add CDN renditions.
  7. Prevention: Macrobenchmark scroll test with FrameTimingMetric; lint/review rule that every image request has a size; alert on average decoded bitmap bytes per image.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just reduce quality" globally; not disable hardware acceleration (worse). Prefetch costs data/memory on low-RAM devices.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Compose version with AsyncImage? → Same upload mechanics; verify size resolution is set from constraints.
  • A hardware bitmap crashes on getPixels? → Hardware bitmaps are immutable and not readable on CPU; copy to software when needed.
  • Why not largeHeap? → Doesn't touch GPU upload time.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A catalog app saw jank only on first scroll after install; the culprit was 3000 px assets from a marketing CMS. A one-line override(width) dropped p95 frame time from 29 ms to 12 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames main thread/bind code.
  • Hire: identifies texture upload and downsizes images.
  • Strong hire: explains upload mechanics and math, prepareToDraw/hardware bitmaps, prefetch trade-offs, and prevents regressions in CI.

questions.promptHtml: What is overdraw, how do you detect it, and does it still matter on modern devices?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Basic GPU fill-rate awareness.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Overdraw is drawing the same pixel more than once in a frame, typically stacked opaque backgrounds. It costs fill-rate on the GPU, which matters on low-end GPUs and at 90/120 Hz. I detect it with Developer options "Debug GPU overdraw" (true color = 1x, blue 1x extra, green 2x, light red 3x, red 4x+), then remove redundant window/parent backgrounds. The framework can cull some obscured opaque draws, but I should not rely on that for translucent stacks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Fill cost is roughly pixels x layers. A 1080x2400 screen is 2.59 M pixels; four layers on all of it is about 10 M pixel shades per frame, at 120 Hz about 1.2 G shades per second before blending cost. Fix list: remove android:background from layers that are fully covered, remove the default window background when the root paints its own (window.setBackgroundDrawable(null) or theme android:windowBackground) but watch for start transitions, avoid full-screen translucent scrims stacked, use clipRect/quickReject, flatten hierarchies. In Compose, stacked Surface/Box with background colors do the same. Symptom in Profile GPU Rendering: tall Swap Buffers/Command Issue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Bad: three opaque fills over the same area
Box(Modifier.fillMaxSize().background(Color.White)) {
    Surface(color = Color.White, modifier = Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
        Column(Modifier.background(Color.White)) { /* ... */ }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Chasing red tint on tiny areas.
  • Removing window background and getting a black flash.
  • Treating overdraw as the cause without GPU evidence in the trace.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a little overdraw okay? → Yes, 2x is common; target avoiding 4x on large areas.
  2. Is overdraw only GPU? → CPU record also grows with extra draw ops.
  3. How would you prove it mattered? → GPU frame time in Perfetto/Profile GPU Rendering before/after.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "turn on the overdraw debug". Senior: ties to fill-rate, device tier and refresh rate, and validates with measurements.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Removing a duplicated white background three levels deep cut GPU time 20% on a low-end 90 Hz tablet.

questions.promptHtml: How do bitmaps become GPU textures, and what do config, size, hardware bitmaps and prepareToDraw() change?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Image-heavy apps jank and OOM here; it ties memory to frame time.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A bitmap displayed by the hardware renderer is uploaded to the GPU as a texture the first time it draws. Cost scales with pixels, not file size: width x height x bytes per pixel (4 for ARGB_8888, 2 for RGB_565). Decode to the displayed size, not the source size. Bitmap.prepareToDraw() (API 24+) triggers the upload early while RenderThread is idle, and HARDWARE bitmaps (API 26+) decode straight to GPU-resident memory, saving the copy but making pixels unreadable from CPU.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Example: 4000x3000 photo = 12 M pixels x 4 = 48 MB decoded; shown in a 360x270 dp (about 1080x810 px at 3x) view needs 3.5 MB. Uploading 48 MB wastes upload time, RAM, and may exceed max texture size (commonly 4096 or 8192; query GL_MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE, device dependent). The Android docs show this as Texture upload(id) width x height in a trace and recommend checking that the bitmap is not much larger than its on-screen area. Loaders (Coil, Glide) size to target and may call prepareToDraw; verify in the library version you use. Config choice: ARGB_8888 default; RGBA_F16 for wide gamut doubles memory; HARDWARE config disallows getPixels, software canvas draws, and some Palette use.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val opts = BitmapFactory.Options().apply { inSampleSize = 4 }
val bmp = BitmapFactory.decodeFile(path, opts)
bmp.prepareToDraw() // API 24+: upload before it is needed (call off main thread after decode)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Decoding full size then letting ImageView scale.
  • Using HARDWARE config then calling copy or drawing into a software Canvas (throws IllegalStateException).
  • Calling prepareToDraw for bitmaps never displayed.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is JPEG file size misleading? → Decoded memory depends on dimensions.
  2. What happens to texture memory on trim? → Textures are evictable/reloaded; re-upload cost appears again as jank.
  3. Bitmap pool role? → Reduces GC churn; separate from texture upload.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use Glide/Coil". Senior: computes decoded and texture bytes, picks config, and knows what the upload costs on RenderThread.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Switching a gallery to HARDWARE bitmaps cut heap use 35% but broke a blur step that read pixels; fixed by copying only for that path.

questions.contextHtml:
A pulsing "live" badge animation was added to a list item. After release, scroll jank rose from 3% to 11% on mid-range devices, and memory use on that screen is up 90 MB. Code from the PR:

class LiveBadgeView(ctx: Context) : FrameLayout(ctx) {
    init { setLayerType(LAYER_TYPE_HARDWARE, null) }

    fun pulse() {
        ObjectAnimator.ofFloat(this, "scaleX", 1f, 1.2f).apply {
            repeatCount = ValueAnimator.INFINITE
            start()
        }
    }
    override fun onDraw(c: Canvas) {
        super.onDraw(c)
        invalidate() // keep it "fresh"
    }
}

Every row in a 200-item list holds one of these. Perfetto shows Record View#draw fine but DrawFrame has long slices with offscreen layer work, and RenderThread GPU memory is high.
questions.promptHtml: Find the problems and explain what each costs.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Layers make it faster, so the problem is the list size." They miss that a hardware layer is an offscreen texture that is only a win when the content is static and the transform is cheap.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the animated child changing content every frame? How many badges are visible at once? Any alpha on parents? Does it jank with the layer removed?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove setLayerType from the item view and the invalidate() in onDraw; ship a hot fix behind a flag.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) invalidate() inside onDraw forces a redraw every frame, which re-renders the layer every frame; the cache is invalidated every time; (b) a hardware layer per row allocates an offscreen texture per view (memory + extra render pass); (c) scale animation on a layer is only cheap if content unchanged; (d) animator never cancelled when row is recycled (leak, red herring for jank but real).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto, offscreen layer slices and GPU memory; Profile GPU Rendering for Command Issue/Swap; toggle Debug hardware layers updates developer option (flashes green when a layer re-renders); heap dump for animators.
  5. Root cause: A hardware layer caches a view's rendering into a texture; it pays off when the view's content is unchanged and only properties like alpha, scale or translation change. Here content invalidates every frame, so every frame we render into the offscreen texture and then composite it: double work, plus per-row texture memory (a 200x200 px layer is only 160 KB, but 8 visible rows with larger bounds and full-width layers adds up; measure in trace).
  6. Fix: Remove the explicit layer; animate with ViewPropertyAnimator/animate().scaleX(...) which can temporarily use a layer for the animation duration (withLayer() on request); cancel animator in onDetachedFromWindow; remove invalidate() from onDraw.
  7. Prevention: Review rule: setLayerType needs a trace-backed reason; Macrobenchmark scroll test; leak check with LeakCanary.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not use LAYER_TYPE_SOFTWARE (CPU rendering, slower and memory heavy). Layer is justified for short animations of static complex content (e.g. alpha-fading a heavy view).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• When is a layer right? → Fading or translating a static complex subtree and overlapping children make alpha look wrong without a layer (hasOverlappingRendering).
  • Compose equivalent? → Modifier.graphicsLayer { } creates a RenderNode; CompositingStrategy.Offscreen forces offscreen only when needed.
  • Why is memory up? → Each layer is a texture sized to the view.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shimmer placeholder with layers on every card made a feed slower than no animation at all; one layer on the container fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: cannot explain layer cost.
  • Hire: finds invalidate-in-onDraw and per-row layers.
  • Strong hire: explains cache validity, uses the layer-update debug option, and gives the Compose analogue.

questions.promptHtml: Explain LAYER_TYPE_NONE, SOFTWARE and HARDWARE. When is each right, and how does graphicsLayer in Compose relate?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Common source of both wins and regressions.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NONE draws the view normally into the parent's display list. HARDWARE renders the view into an offscreen GPU texture and then composites it, which is cheap to move, fade or scale if content does not change. SOFTWARE renders into a CPU bitmap, only for features hardware renderer cannot do; it is slow and memory heavy. In Compose, Modifier.graphicsLayer makes a RenderNode with properties (alpha, scale, translation, rotation) updated in the draw phase without recomposition or relayout.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Costs of a HARDWARE layer: allocation of texture sized to view bounds, a render pass to fill it, memory, and a re-render each time the view invalidates. Benefit: animating transform/alpha property applies on RenderThread without re-running view draw. View.animate() can use withLayer(); the framework for alpha with overlapping content may implicitly use a layer (hasOverlappingRendering(); returning false avoids the offscreen layer when children do not overlap). Software layers were once needed for unsupported operations (some Canvas ops), and have limits like no hardware acceleration for the layer's content; avoid on modern API levels. In Compose: graphicsLayer { alpha = ... } lambda reads state in draw phase; compositingStrategy = CompositingStrategy.Offscreen enables offscreen compositing when needed, with default Auto using it only if alpha < 1 (verify per release).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Box(Modifier.graphicsLayer {
    translationY = scrollState.value * 0.5f   // read in draw phase: no recomposition
    alpha = fade.value
})

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Leaving a hardware layer permanently set.
  • Layers on views that update every frame.
  • Reading state outside the lambda form and recomposing.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is hasOverlappingRendering? → Tells the framework whether alpha needs an offscreen layer for correctness.
  2. Why avoid software layers? → CPU rendering and bitmap memory.
  3. How can you see layer re-renders? → Developer option "Show hardware layers updates".

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "layers cache the view". Senior: states when the cache is valid, the offscreen cost, and the Compose draw-phase equivalent.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Flipping a fading header to a single graphicsLayer alpha removed per-frame recomposition during scroll.

questions.promptHtml: What is shader compilation jank on Android, why does it hit the first use of an effect, and what can an app do about it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests GPU-pipeline understanding beyond CPU tracing: one-time spikes with a clean main thread.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: GPU programs (shaders/pipelines) are compiled lazily by the driver the first time a draw needs them. That compile is on the RenderThread and can take tens of milliseconds, so the first time a new effect, gradient, blur, clip or AGSL RuntimeShader appears I see one long DrawFrame while the main thread is clean. Later frames are fine. The platform caches compiled shaders on disk, so the pain is concentrated in the first run after install, update or cache clear. App-side I reduce unique shader variants, warm up off-screen at a safe moment, and verify with traces.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Pipeline: draw op requires a shader program variant (combination of paint features like gradient + clip + blend) -> if not in in-memory/disk cache, the driver compiles -> RenderThread blocks. Evidence: a single DrawFrame slice of 40-80 ms (one anecdotal source puts first-frame compile at that order; treat as illustrative) with GPU-related child slices and no repeat on second run. I could not find official Android docs on HWUI's cache internals, so describe behavior as observed and say "verify on your device/OS". Mitigations: (1) reuse a small set of effects/brushes instead of many unique ones; (2) AGSL RuntimeShader (API 33+) compiles per shader; create once and reuse, do not rebuild per frame; (3) pre-warm by drawing the effect once in a tiny offscreen/invisible layer during idle after launch; (4) Baseline Profiles help code (ART) not shaders, so do not claim they fix this; (5) test cold install on a clean device, not a reused phone.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// AGSL (API 33+): create once, update uniforms per frame
private val shader = RuntimeShader(AGSL_SRC)          // compile cost once
fun draw(c: Canvas, t: Float) {
    shader.setFloatUniform("time", t)                 // cheap
    paint.shader = shader
    c.drawRect(bounds, paint)
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Recreating RuntimeShader/Paint shaders in onDraw.
  • Declaring "cannot reproduce" because the dev device has warm caches.
  • Claiming Baseline Profiles remove shader jank.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you reproduce reliably? → Clear app data or fresh install, reboot, run the animation, Perfetto.
  2. Why does it look "random" in vitals? → It appears only on first use per install/OS update.
  3. Can a pre-warm backfire? → Yes: if done on main/critical path or visible, it moves the jank to launch.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "GPU spike". Senior: explains lazy driver compile, cache lifetime, and a repro protocol with clean-install traces.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A blur+gradient hero transition showed 3% of users with a 60 ms stall only on first open after update; a one-time idle warm-up removed it.

questions.contextHtml: A video-first social app (6M DAU) ships a new feed card with rounded video thumbnails, a gradient scrim and a blurred avatar background. Within 48 hours Vitals shows slow-frame rate for the feed jump from 3% to 8%, but dashboard breakdown says: flagship devices 2%, mid-tier 4%, and one chipset family (Mali GPU, 3-4 GB RAM, 90 Hz panels) 21%. Support forwards a screen recording: smooth for a second, then rhythmic stutter. The main-thread doFrame is 6-7 ms in a trace from a repro device. dumpsys gfxinfo shows high "Slow issue draw commands" and the Swap Buffers bar is tall. A teammate suggests lowering list prefetch distance.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and decide what to do for that device class.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Optimize onBind and RecyclerView prefetch." They follow the red herring: the main thread is fine and the evidence points to GPU/RenderThread.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it only at 90 Hz (budget 11.1 ms)? Which jank type in FrameTimeline? Does thermal throttling start after about a minute (matches "smooth then stutter")? Did the Mali family jank before this release?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-flag the blurred background off and use a static tint for that device group, keyed on GPU/chipset or a measured frame-time heuristic.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) GPU-bound: blur (RenderEffect/saveLayer) + clipping rounded video + scrim = multiple offscreen passes and overdraw at 90 Hz; (b) thermal throttle reducing GPU clock; (c) SF GPU composition from extra layers (video surface + overlays); (d) bind work (red herring: trace says 6 ms).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto with GPU counters/FrameTimeline jank type (AppDeadlineMissed vs SurfaceFlingerGpuDeadlineMissed); DrawFrame slice breakdown for offscreen/saveLayer; Profile GPU Rendering Swap Buffers; the same scroll with effect toggled, A/B on a loaner device; check thermal state/PowerManager.getCurrentThermalStatus() (API 29+).
  5. Root cause (example outcome): GPU time per frame exceeds 11 ms on this tier: the blur samples a large region, rounded-clip forces an offscreen pass per video card, plus a full-width translucent scrim; 3 cards visible means multiple full-pass costs, and throttling worsens after a minute.
  6. Fix: Short term: gate blur by device tier/frame health; replace clip with RoundedCornerShape via drawing the rounded rect with a shader/outlineProvider where hardware supports it. Long term: pre-blur at image-load time (cached bitmap) instead of runtime blur; reduce layers; adaptive quality using JankStats feedback.
  7. Prevention: Device-tier matrix in Macrobenchmark/firebase test lab for at least one Mali mid-tier; vitals alert segmented by chipset; design review requires GPU cost note for blur/clip.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not ship a global downgrade (hurts flagships); not blame the OEM driver before proving it with a trace; adaptive degrade adds code paths to test.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why was the lab green? → CI ran flagship emulators/devices; no mid-tier GPU, no thermals.
  • Could Compose Modifier.blur be cheaper? → API 31+ uses RenderEffect; below that it has no effect; it still costs GPU.
  • Lower refresh rate instead? → Possible via frame rate hint/category API, but trading smoothness; last resort.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: One feature passed on every lab phone and failed on a popular mid-range chipset; a $150 loaner phone in the CI farm paid for itself in one sprint.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes RecyclerView.
  • Hire: identifies GPU/RenderThread bound using trace and gates the effect per device.
  • Strong hire: separates jank types, accounts for refresh rate and thermals, proposes pre-computation and device-tier test coverage.

questions.contextHtml: Your manager says: "Play Console shows slow rendering at 14% of sessions, the bar is 8%. Fix jank." The app has 40 screens, a 4-person team and two weeks. Dashboard data: slow frames by screen are unavailable; you have JankStats not yet integrated, a Macrobenchmark module exists for startup only, and several devs say "the feed is slow". No repro steps exist.
questions.promptHtml: How do you turn this into a plan and what do you deliver in week one?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Profile the feed and optimize it." This assumes the answer without evidence and ignores that vitals counts sessions, not screens.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which vitals metric exactly (slow sessions percent: sessions with 25%+ frames over 16 ms per Play definition, verify current), which device and OS cuts, and is the goal passing the bad-behavior threshold or user-visible smoothness?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is not an outage. Avoid risky changes before instrumentation.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Feed/list screens, startup transition frames (frozen frames are tracked separately), one low-end device cluster, one heavy animation screen.
  4. How I'd verify each: Day 1-2: integrate JankStats with screen/list state tags, aggregate per screen and device tier and ship; add Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric scroll tests for the top 3 screens; manual gfxinfo runs on one low-end device.
  5. Root cause: Unknown until data; expected a Pareto where 2-3 screens give most jank.
  6. Fix: Week 2: fix top findings by Perfetto evidence; keep each change measured before/after.
  7. Prevention: Jank budget per screen in CI, dashboard by screen/device, regression alert.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite the feed first; not optimize by feel; accept that field data needs a release cycle to arrive, so also reproduce locally in parallel.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Metric will not move for weeks after fix? → Rollout lag; use staged rollout and compare cohorts.
  • Frozen vs slow? → Frozen frames (over 700 ms) at startup/transition get priority; per Android docs they are tracked separately.
  • Manager wants a date? → Commit to the measurement and a target, not to the number.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Instrumenting first revealed 70% of jank came from a settings screen with an infinite shimmer nobody had profiled.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts optimizing blindly.
  • Hire: instruments then prioritizes.
  • Strong hire: defines metric, segments by device, sets budgets and a verification loop with before/after.

questions.promptHtml: How do variable and high refresh rates change jank analysis, and what is frame pacing / buffer stuffing about?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Modern devices switch rates dynamically; naive 16.6 ms thinking breaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: On VRR/adaptive panels the system picks a refresh rate (e.g. 60/90/120) per content and touch, so the deadline moves under my feet. I should compare frame time against the actual rate and use FrameTimeline's expected vs actual times rather than a fixed 16.6. Frame pacing means frames are presented evenly; uneven pacing (a 12 ms then 25 ms frame) looks janky even if average is fine. Buffer stuffing means the app queues frames faster than they can be shown, adding latency without visible drops.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html: Budget table: 60 Hz 16.67 ms, 90 Hz 11.11 ms, 120 Hz 8.33 ms. Android lets apps hint a preferred rate with Surface.setFrameRate() / SurfaceControl.Transaction.setFrameRate (API 30+); newer releases add frame-rate categories (verify API level). JankStats default heuristic is 2x the current refresh interval, so thresholds adapt. Perfetto shows expected vs actual timeline per frame, prediction by the scheduler. A game-style render loop that ignores Choreographer should use Frame Pacing Library. Buffer stuffing: app is ahead by more than one buffer; fixes involve not rendering ahead of vsync (e.g. avoid dequeueing early, use Choreographer timing, avoid unbounded producers such as camera/video overlays).

sections.label: Code
sections.html: n/a

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Hard-coding 16 ms in tests and lint thresholds.
  • Forcing 120 Hz everywhere (battery, thermal).
  • Equating buffer stuffing with dropped frames.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can 120 Hz make animations worse? → Same cost per frame but half the budget.
  2. What is a good rate hint use? → Video at 24/30 fps content declares so; static screens allow lower rates.
  3. How do you measure pacing, not just average? → p95/p99 frame durations and FrameTimeline per-frame delta.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "16 ms". Senior: refresh-rate-relative thresholds, pacing, stuffing and latency trade-offs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A fixed 16.6 ms assert in a UI test hid failures on 120 Hz devices for months.

questions.contextHtml: Your app's "story viewer" has p95 frame time of 9.8 ms on 60 Hz test devices, 0.4% janky frames. Marketing launches in a market where 55% of new phones are 120 Hz (up from 8% in your current base). Beta data from 120 Hz devices: 12% janky frames on swipe between stories, p95 9.5 ms, p99 21 ms. JankStats states point at "Story=Transition". Perfetto: main-thread doFrame sits at 6-9 ms; DrawFrame 2-3 ms; occasional 20 ms outliers with GC on HeapTaskDaemon and Binder calls. Product wants the launch on time.
questions.promptHtml: What changes at 120 Hz, and what is your plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "p95 is 9.5 ms, under 16.6 so it's fine." Wrong budget: 120 Hz gives 8.33 ms.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the device actually running 120 Hz during the transition (adaptive switching)? Is jank classified AppDeadlineMissed? Are outliers GC/Binder or steady cost? Which tiers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Use a frame-rate hint (e.g. Surface.setFrameRate, API 30+) or cap transition effects, only if smoothness at 60 is acceptable; reduce transition cost for launch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) steady cost 6-9 ms main plus 2-3 ms render exceeds 8.33 ms; (b) allocation-driven GC pauses in the 20 ms outliers; (c) binder calls (e.g. repeated Display.getRefreshRate()) stalling UI thread; (d) SF composition for layered video (red herring until proven).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto FrameTimeline on a 120 Hz device; allocation profiler during swipe; adb shell am trace-ipc for binder; Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric on 120 Hz device for baseline.
  5. Root cause: Steady frame cost 8.5-11 ms was fine at 16.6 and exceeds 8.33; frames fit only half the time. Outliers add stalls.
  6. Fix: Cut main-thread work (precompute layout, avoid per-frame allocations, cache binder results), move transition properties to RenderThread-friendly properties (translation/alpha via graphicsLayer/ViewPropertyAnimator), pre-decode next story image.
  7. Prevention: Test matrix includes 120 Hz; thresholds relative to refresh rate; allocation budget in review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Do not lock 60 Hz globally (feels worse on flagship); do not claim 120 fps everywhere is a goal; battery/thermal matter.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Emulator shows no issue? → Emulators rarely model real GPU/CPU and VRR.
  • Can the OS drop to 60 for you? → The system may choose, but you cannot rely on it.
  • How to explain to PM? → "Every frame has half the time; we must halve cost or accept lower rate on this screen."

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A swipe animation that was perfect at 60 Hz became the top complaint after a flagship launch; trimming three allocations per frame fixed 80% of it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: uses 16.6 ms.
  • Hire: recomputes budget, finds cost via trace.
  • Strong hire: handles outliers (GC/binder), rate hints, and refresh-aware CI.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident: after release 8.4, scroll jank in Settings-heavy screens rose from 2% to 7% on Android 13-14 devices, with ANR rate unchanged (0.2%). Perfetto traces show Choreographer#doFrame stretching to 25-40 ms, but the main thread's state is mostly "Sleeping" with binder transaction slices of 8-30 ms. The offending call stack (from am trace-ipc) repeatedly hits PackageManager.getApplicationInfo and Display.getRefreshRate() from a custom view's onMeasure, introduced by a refactor that moved a cached value into a getter. A teammate wants to "profile the CPU more" because CPU use looks low.
questions.promptHtml: Write the incident review: how it was found, root cause, and prevention.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Main thread was slow, so optimize methods." CPU profile shows nothing because the thread was blocked, not running.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed between 8.3 and 8.4? Does it correlate with OS version/OEM? Is it steady or bursty? Which threads hold the binder server side?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hot fix: cache the values at init and remove from onMeasure; staged rollout.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) binder calls on UI thread blocked on system_server; (b) lock contention with a background thread; (c) GC (ruled out by trace); (d) thread scheduling (runnable-but-not-running slices would be blue; check).
  4. How I'd verify each: Perfetto thread state track (Sleeping vs Runnable vs Running), binder slices with peer process, adb shell am trace-ipc start/stop to capture stacks (documented in Android docs), StrictMode on debug builds.
  5. Root cause: A hot path (onMeasure, called many times per frame) made synchronous IPC. Each call waits on system_server, whose latency varies with system load. Android docs note even innocuous calls such as getRefreshRate() can be binder transactions and hurt when frequent.
  6. Fix: Cache outside measure/draw; read once per attach or on DisplayListener change; move info lookups off main thread.
  7. Prevention: Custom lint/detekt rule banning system service lookups in onMeasure/onDraw; Macrobenchmark with trace analysis of binder counts; StrictMode in dev; add custom trace sections.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Don't sprinkle trace markers on tiny methods (about 10 µs overhead each per docs guidance, avoid for calls under about 200 µs); don't only rely on CPU profiler for blocked time.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not an ANR? → Each call is short; no single 5 s block.
  • How to catch in prod? → JankStats state + sampled system traces; custom counters of binder per frame (hard); Perfetto in-field via ProfilingManager (API 35+, verify).
  • Lock instead of binder? → Thread state and monitor contention slices show it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A harmless-looking context.resources.displayMetrics-adjacent call replaced with a service lookup doubled frame time on one OEM's slower system_server.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: CPU-only analysis.
  • Hire: reads thread states and finds binder.
  • Strong hire: gives complete incident review, tooling, lint guardrails.

questions.promptHtml: Describe your method for reading a janky frame in a Perfetto trace, top to bottom.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The core senior skill: turning a trace into a root cause in minutes.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I start with FrameTimeline to find janky frames and their jank type, then pick one and see which side missed: app or SurfaceFlinger. For an app miss I go to the main thread's Choreographer#doFrame, split into input/animation/traversal (measure, layout, Record View#draw), then to RenderThread DrawFrame and GPU/fence waits. I always look at thread state (Running vs Sleeping vs Runnable) to decide between "my code is slow", "blocked" and "descheduled". Then I add custom trace sections and re-capture.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Steps:

  1. Capture on a release-like build: Perfetto/System Tracing with gfx, view, sched, binder_driver, freq categories; -a <package> style app tracing for RecyclerView markers.
  2. Expected vs Actual timeline rows for the app process; red/jank-typed frames.
  3. Main thread: long doFrame children. Record View#draw long means custom draw or CPU bitmap work; Layout long means nesting/double taxation or layout every frame; Input/animation long means callbacks.
  4. RenderThread: syncFrameState, Texture upload, flush commands, eglSwapBuffers/dequeue; GPU fence waits mean GPU-bound.
  5. Thread state: blue (Runnable) = CPU contention/scheduling; red/orange = uninterruptible sleep (I/O); gray = sleeping/waiting (locks, binder).
  6. Cross-check with CPU frequency and big/little core placement for thermal/scheduler effects.
  7. Hypothesis, instrument with Trace.beginSection, retest.
janky frame -> app or SF? -> main thread doFrame breakdown -> RenderThread -> GPU -> thread state

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import androidx.tracing.trace
trace("FeedCard#bind") { bindCard(item) }  // androidx.tracing:tracing-ktx

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reading a debug-build trace.
  • Starting from the longest slice instead of the janky frame.
  • Method-tracing (profiler) to find jank (distorts timing).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just CPU Profiler? → Method traces add overhead and cannot show blocked vs running well, per Android docs.
  2. How to tell scheduling delay? → Long Runnable time before Running.
  3. How to compare builds? → Same device, same scenario, Macrobenchmark traces and SQL aggregates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: opens trace, looks at long slices. Senior: has a repeatable top-down procedure and uses thread states and FrameTimeline.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 4-line SQL query over Macrobenchmark traces found the one screen with Texture upload over 4 ms across 30 runs.

questions.contextHtml: Release regressions keep slipping: three releases in a row increased feed jank by 2-5 points; QA only notices by eye. You must design an automated gate within one sprint. Constraints: 20 PRs/day, CI has two physical low-end devices (60 Hz) and one 120 Hz phone; Macrobenchmark scroll test takes about 4 min per device per run; observed run-to-run noise on p90 frame time is about +/-8%; budget for device minutes is limited.
questions.promptHtml: Design the gate. What do you measure, where does it run, and how do you avoid flakiness and alert fatigue?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Fail the PR if janky frames exceed 5%." Single threshold, no noise handling, no device tiering, runs on emulators.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which journeys are business critical? What is the acceptable regression? Can we get more devices? Who owns triage?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Start with a nightly job on main, not per-PR, for the top 2 journeys; alert-only for two weeks to learn noise.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Not applicable; design decisions: metric (frame duration p50/p90/p99 and frame overrun via Macrobenchmark FrameTimingMetric: frameDurationCpuMs, frameOverrunMs on API 31+), compilation mode (CompilationMode.Partial with baseline profile to mimic production), iterations (10+), device lab.
  4. How I'd verify each: Run A/A comparisons (same commit twice) to measure noise; compare medians across iterations with a statistical threshold (e.g., regression flagged if p90 worse than baseline by more than noise band, derived from A/A data, not a guess).
  5. Root cause: Regressions slip because there is no objective, repeatable measure tied to commits.
  6. Fix: Nightly baseline with history; per-PR smoke only for PRs touching list/UI modules (path filters) plus a bisect job; store Perfetto traces as artifacts so failures are debuggable; JankStats field metrics as the source of truth for the budget.
  7. Prevention: Owners per journey, budgets in repo, dashboard, auto-bisect on regression, quarantining flaky tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not per-PR on every commit (cost, noise); not emulators; not a single absolute threshold; a gate that blocks randomly will be disabled, so start non-blocking.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Noise too high? → More iterations, pin CPU/thermal state (cooldown), fixed brightness/airplane mode, rerun on failure.
  • 120 Hz only issue? → Keep one 120 Hz device in the nightly matrix.
  • Lab vs field disagree? → Field wins for prioritization; lab for diagnosis.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gate with ±3% threshold flapped daily until an A/A study showed ±8% noise; widening the band plus 15 iterations made it trustworthy.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: fixed threshold on emulator.
  • Hire: Macrobenchmark on real devices with iterations.
  • Strong hire: measured noise, tiered devices, trace artifacts, staged blocking policy.
